sections.COMMENTS:
This Composite Source is located in the southern Garda Lake area and connects the NE-SW trending Giudicarie thrust system to the north with the outer, E-W trending Southern Alps thrust fronts buried in the plain. This source was mapped using the interpretation of seismic lines, constrained by residual Bouguer gravimetric anomaly maps. This source has been established within the research developed during the European Project GeoMol (http://www.geomol.eu/).
In the northern sector of the Po Plain, the external thrusts of the Southern Alps form a broad S-verging arc that connects a roughly E-W trending front buried in the plain with the NE-striking faults of the Giudicarie thrust system. However, recent subsurface data highlights that the lateral continuity of this systems is interrupted south of the Garda Lake by the presence of NW-SE trending Mesozoic inherited normal faults. These structures are rooted in the sedimentary basement and have the same depth range of the Southern Alps thrusts currently included in DISS as seismogenic sources, thus segmenting them.
The seismic lines crossing this area together with other geophysical data show that the connection between the two thrust systems is in reality a quite complex area, imaging two ca. 30 km long, WNW-ESE striking, S-verging thrusts (the Sirmione and the Solferino thrusts, to the north and south, respectively), located slightly to the north respect to the area occupied by the NW-trending inherited normal faults. In the same area, a map of the residual Bouguer gravimetric anomaly shows two right-stepping en-echelon gravimetric highs that highlight the anticlines related to the Sirmione and Solferino thrusts, and hence help defining the geometry at depth of the southern part of the Giudicarie Fault System.
Historical and instrumental catalogues show that this area is characterized by a scattered distribution of low magnitude events, apart from the 1222 Basso Bresciano earthquake that however have been associated with the Southern Alps outer thrusts located more to the west.
The strike of this source was taken from subsurface geophysical data; the dip was inferred from regional geological consideration concerning the thrust plane. The rake was assumed to represent pure thrusting, based on general geodynamic considerations. The minimum and maximum depth were based on that of nearby sources and on the uncertainty concerning the depth at which active thrusting is rooted. The slip rate was inferred from regional geodynamic data.

pictures.c: Interpreted regional seismic reflection profiles straddling the full extents of the Adriatic basin, including the Po Plain and the adjacent Northern Apennines (to the west), Southern Alps (to the north), and Dinarides (to the east) (from Fantoni and Franciosi [2009]).

pictures.t: Structural map of the central-eastern Po Plain
pictures.c: Structural map of the central and eastern Po Plain, showing the different fault systems with different colors. The Mesozoic inherited normal faults that are believed to have controlled the propagation and geometry of Northern Apennines and Southern Alps thrust fronts are shown in blue (from Scardia et al. [2014]).

pictures.t: Seismic profiles from the central-eastern Po Plain
pictures.c: Seismic profiles and their interpretation showing the buried structures of the Po Plain south of the Garda Lake (from Scardia et al. [2014]).

pictures.t: Seismotectonic model of the central Po Plain
pictures.c: Seismotectonic model of the central Po Plain showing the possible interplay between the Mesozoic inherited normal faults, interpreted to be reactivated in the present-day stress regime as right-lateral strike slip faults, and the thrust fronts of the Southern Alps (from Scardia et al. [2014]).
